title: Call my (estate) agent! Why celebrities are always buying each other’s homes
text:
Last year, Austin Butler bought a mansion from Brad Pitt. The month before, Brad Pitt bought a mansion from one of the Killers. In 2022, Adele bought Sylvester Stallone’s old house, but only if he let her keep his Rocky statue. Aaron Paul recently sold a house that he bought from The Big Bang Theory’s Jim Parsons, who bought it from Robert Pattinson, after it was previously owned by Noah Wyle, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Tim Curry and the guy who directed Legally Blonde.
If this makes it sound to you as if there are only a handful of celebrity-friendly homes on earth, and celebrities spend their lives swapping them around among themselves, then you’re right.
According to Mohamed Mussa, the managing director of Chestertons Global, this is partly by design. In an op-ed that has been doing the rounds, Mussa explains that celebrities often require things in properties that civilians like us might not consider, such as gated entrances, secluded grounds, space for staff and layouts designed to keep fans at bay.
“In 2020, Los Angeles City Council passed an ordinance allowing tour buses to be banned from residential streets judged unsafe,” he explains, which has to be useful. I once had a fairly major freakout after buying my house because I didn’t check the details properly and missed that the plumbing under my kitchen sink consisted of an Evian bottle sellotaped to a pipe. Imagine how much worse it would be to buy a house and realise that a packed bus parks outside your front door three times a day so that tourists can try and take a picture of you putting the washing out.
In other words, it helps a celebrity to know that a celebrity used to live there because, as Mussa states, a property’s ownership history “can also offer a useful indication of how well the home accommodates the demands of a high-profile lifestyle”.
You may have also noticed that a lot of these celebrity homes never reached the open market. According to Mussa, this is also by design. “Drake bought Robbie Williams’ Beverly Crest estate in 2022 in an off-market deal, illustrating how a transaction can take place privately,” he writes. “At this level, buyers, sellers and their trusted advisers form a small ecosystem, connecting people with similar lifestyles and property requirements, sometimes before a home is ever advertised. This network helps explain how certain properties pass from one high-profile owner to another, with each new buyer looking for many of the same things as the last.”
Of course, the big benefit of doing this is that you avoid a public listing. This is preferential, because once your home goes up on Zoopla, then every casual rubbernecker on the face of the planet can click around and see the untrammelled depths of your berserk self-absorption. To be clear, I am talking about Joe Pesci here.
In 2019, Joe Pesci listed his eight bedroom Jersey Shore mansion for $6.5m. But he did it publicly, which meant that a gallery went online. How do we know the home belonged to Joe Pesci, you ask? Well, the subtle clues were there all along.
There was a barber chair near the front door, because Pesci worked as a barber in the 1960s. There was a music room, because Joe Pesci once recorded an entire album in character as the guy he played in My Cousin Vinny. Then there was a room containing 12 separate posters for Joe Pesci movies, a full-sized Lethal Weapon 3 pinball table and a framed poster-sized photo of Joe Pesci winning an Oscar for Goodfellas, although strangely not the Oscar itself. It is also worth pointing out that one of the rooms in Joe Pesci’s house contained a giant printed-out meme of Joe Pesci and the caption: “If U ain’t adding to this shit don’t ask me for shit.”
Could this have been avoided if Pesci had followed Mussa’s advice and sold the property to another celebrity off the books? Almost certainly. Did seeing the photos of Pesci’s home make me wish that I could buy it and live there in its Pesci-era state? Definitely. But was the home demolished as soon as Pesci moved out four years ago? Sadly yes. And has knowing this left me in a state of bleak despondency? Also yes.
